IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

Russia is running an active influence operation targeting the 2026 midterms. That part is documented. The more important story is what comes after the disclosure.

Start with the detection problem. The Election Threats Executive Group is gone or effectively gutted. The interagency coordination machinery that existed in 2020 has been stripped down. So the operation is running into an environment where the early-warning architecture is weaker than it has been at any point since 2016. Disclosure happened through journalism, not through government detection and public attribution. That is a meaningful shift. It means the response timeline compresses badly, because by the time reporting confirms a campaign, it has already been running.

Now look at the tradecraft evolution, because that is what actually matters for the next eighteen months.

The 2018 operation required large human operator teams to generate volume. The 2022 operation was more efficient but still recognizable by the signature of coordinated inauthentic behavior: accounts moving in lockstep, posting at patterns that don't match organic human activity, translated idioms. The 2026 operation is documented as using AI-enhanced content generation. What that means operationally is smaller teams producing more content at higher quality with fewer of the linguistic tells that platform trust and safety teams trained their detection on. The old detection signatures are degrading in usefulness. The platforms have not yet published updated detection frameworks that account for this, and several of them have reduced the teams that would build those frameworks.

The targeting is also worth watching closely. The reported focus on suppressing Democratic voter enthusiasm and turnout is consistent with a shift away from the 2016-era strategy of broad polarization for polarization's sake. The 2026 targeting is more surgical. Economic anxiety and cost-of-living narratives are being used as the entry point. That is smart operational design. Those narratives are grounded in real conditions. They don't require fabrication to land, they just require framing. A voter seeing content that says their grocery bill is high because of Democratic governance isn't necessarily seeing a lie. They're seeing a selective frame delivered at scale by a foreign actor with a stake in the outcome. That's much harder to counter than a fabricated story about a candidate, because the counter-argument doesn't begin with "that's false."

The demographic micro-targeting piece deserves more attention than it's getting. The reporting notes that the operation identifies specific demographic segments susceptible to particular narrative framings. This is not novel in concept, but the AI-enhancement of content generation means the operation can now produce tailored content for those segments at a scale and speed that wasn't achievable in 2018. A Black voter in Georgia, a union household in Michigan, a young male voter anywhere who has migrated to platforms with lighter moderation: each of those segments gets different content, built to land differently. The operational overhead of that kind of targeting has dropped significantly. Which means the targeting will get more granular, not less.

The platform environment is a structural problem that isn't going to resolve before November 2026. Reduced trust and safety investment at the major platforms, combined with altered content moderation philosophies, means the coordinated industry response that characterized 2020 is not the baseline assumption anymore. In 2020, platforms were investing heavily in this, coordinating with each other and with government, and still running removal operations in the weeks before the election. That infrastructure has been partially dismantled. The Russian operation in 2026 is landing into that changed environment intentionally. The timing is not coincidental.

What defenders should actually be watching:

Platform-level detection of coordinated behavior will be slower and less comprehensive than in 2020. That means the operational window for the Russian campaign is longer before meaningful disruption. Watch for whether any of the major platforms publish transparency reports on influence operation takedowns in the six months before the midterms. The absence of such reports will be informative.

The journalism-based disclosure model that surfaced this operation is going to be under pressure. Investigative reporting on foreign interference is expensive, slow, and often legally complicated. Without government attribution to anchor the reporting, outlets have to build the case independently. That is harder, and some operations will not get disclosed on a timeline that is useful for voter awareness.

The use of authentic American political grievances as raw material is going to make legal and regulatory responses nearly impossible before November 2026. Content that is factually selective but not fabricated sits in a gray zone that neither platform policy nor federal law handles well. Expect the operation to stay in that gray zone deliberately.

State-level election officials are not well-resourced to fill the gap left by the federal infrastructure reductions. The Election Assistance Commission has limited authority. The FBI field offices that would normally handle threat communication to local officials are operating in an environment where that kind of proactive engagement has become politically complicated. The result is that the people running the actual mechanics of the election in competitive districts will have less threat-relevant information than they had in 2020. That is a real operational advantage for the Russians, and it compounds over time.

One thing that isn't discussed enough: the Russian operation does not need to change vote totals to succeed. Measurable success metrics for this kind of campaign include reduced turnout in targeted demographics, increased distrust in electoral institutions, and the amplification of post-election disputes regardless of outcome. All of those outcomes are achievable without touching a single voting machine. The campaign is already running. Some of those effects are already accumulating.

The question for the next eighteen months isn't whether the operation exists. It's whether the detection and attribution infrastructure that was stripped back can be partially reconstituted, whether platforms will invest in disclosure even in the absence of government pressure to do so, and whether journalists can maintain the bandwidth to surface operations that government is no longer reliably surfacing. Right now the answer to all three is uncertain, which is exactly the operating environment Russia planned for.

France 24. BBC. Reuters. Al Jazeera. Washington DC. Human Rights Watch.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules. 

This is not policy. This is contempt of constitutional precedent.

The government will say this is about deepfakes. About national security. About public order.

But when 138 YouTube videos were taken down for allegedly defaming Adani, a private businessman, it stopped being about security a long time ago.

France 24 is not attacking India. France 24 is holding up a mirror.

The question is, why is this government so terrified of what Indians might see in it?

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

📰 PRESS FREEDOM AND ACCOUNTABILITY: THE RAVI NAIR DEFAMATION VERDICT

#NewDelhi & #Ahmedabad | Media & Law

A Gujarat trial court’s conviction of journalist Ravi Nair in a criminal-defamation case filed by Adani Enterprises has renewed debate over the boundary between press freedom, investigative journalism and accountability for unverified allegations.

In February 2026, a magistrate’s court in Mansa, Gandhinagar, sentenced Nair to one year’s imprisonment and imposed a fine over social-media posts concerning the Adani Group. According to the court order reported by Reuters, the posts contained allegations relating to political patronage, financial irregularities and unethical conduct.

The trial court reportedly concluded that no documentary material, official record or verified data had been produced to substantiate the serious allegations made against the complainant company.

Nair’s lawyer argued that the posts were based on publicly available information and constituted fair comment and criticism. Nair subsequently stated that he intended to appeal. The judgment is therefore a trial-court determination and remains open to challenge through the appellate process.

⚖️ THE LARGER QUESTION

Freedom of expression is fundamental to democracy. Journalists must remain free to investigate governments, corporations and other powerful institutions. However, freedom of the press does not eliminate the professional obligation to:

🔹 verify serious allegations before publication;
🔹 distinguish facts from allegations and opinions;
🔹 seek and publish the response of the accused party;
🔹 disclose relevant conflicts of interest;
🔹 correct material inaccuracies promptly; and
🔹 avoid sensational headlines unsupported by evidence.

Articles commissioned or influenced by political, ideological, corporate or financial interests—without transparent disclosure—undermine public trust. Repetition by a prominent domestic or international publication does not automatically convert an allegation into an established fact.

At the same time, defamation law must be applied cautiously and proportionately. Corporations, governments and influential individuals should not use prolonged litigation, excessive damages or criminal proceedings merely to discourage legitimate public-interest reporting.

Press-freedom organisations, including the Committee to Protect Journalists, have expressed concern that imprisonment for defamation can produce a chilling effect on investigative journalism. That concern must also form part of an honest discussion.

The democratic balance lies neither in journalistic immunity nor in censorship.

It lies in protecting good-faith investigation while holding demonstrably false, malicious or recklessly unverified publications accountable through fair judicial procedures.

📌 THE PRINCIPLE

A press credential is not immunity from the law. Equally, wealth and political influence must never create immunity from scrutiny.

Free speech protects investigation and dissent—but its credibility rests on evidence, verification, context and the right of reply..

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia 

#Samsung #SamsungIndia #GalaxyS25Ultra #SamsungService #Nagpur #ConsumerRights #scamservice

What are ALPRs

Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs or LPRs) are AI-powered cameras that capture and analyze images of all passing vehicles, storing details like your car's location, date, and time. 
They also capture your car's make, model, color, and identifying features such as dents, roof racks, and bumper stickers, often turning these into searchable data points.

These cameras collect data on millions of vehicles regardless of whether the driver is suspected of a crime. 
These systems are marketed as indispensable tools to fight crime, but they ignore the powerful tools police already have to track criminals, such as cell phone location data, creating a loophole that doesn't require a warrant.

Example of an annotated license plate reader photo showing captured vehicle details
The Dangers of ALPRs
Privacy Violations
ALPRs track your movements and store your data for long periods of time, creating a detailed record of your location history.
Risk of Misuse
Data from ALPRs has led to wrongful arrests, profiling, and stalking ex-partners by police officers.
Limited Benefits
There's no substantial evidence that ALPRs effectively prevent crime, despite Flock's unethical attempts to prove otherwise.

ALPRs are a serious risk to your privacy and civil liberties. 
These systems continuously record your movements without a warrant, probable cause, or even reasonable suspicion. 
Your driving history is rarely confined to the town or city where the cameras are installed. 
It's typically shared with thousands of other agencies nationwide (secretly). 
Once the data is out of your community, you have no control over how it's used or what rules apply, leading to instances of misuse.
What is Flock?

Flock Safety is one of the largest ALPR vendors in the United States. 
Their cameras are installed for police departments, businesses, and HOAs. 
Captured vehicle data is uploaded to Flock's cloud system, where participating agencies can search and share information across jurisdictions.

Flock is not the only ALPR vendor, and other vendors still participate in similar practices. See this list of other common ALPR vendors.

What are ALPRs?

Video explanation of modern LPRs by Christophe

Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs or LPRs) are AI-powered cameras that capture and analyze images of all passing vehicles, storing details like your car's location, date, and time. They also capture your car's make, model, color, and identifying features such as dents, roof racks, and bumper stickers, often turning these into searchable data points.

These cameras collect data on millions of vehicles regardless of whether the driver is suspected of a crime. These systems are marketed as indispensable tools to fight crime, but they ignore the powerful tools police already have to track criminals, such as cell phone location data, creating a loophole that doesn't require a warrant.

For a detailed explanation of how ALPRs are a threat to privacy, see this ACLU article as well as this EFF article on ALPRs.

On August 28, 2026, two patients who had come to Savanur Taluk Hospital in Haveri district, Karnataka, for treatment were allegedly made to manually remove human waste from an overflowing sewage/cesspit on the hospital premises.

According to police and media reports, the patients were allegedly asked to inspect the overflowing sewage and subsequently began clearing the waste using buckets provided by the hospital. Police said they were allegedly offered better medical treatment and medicines in exchange for doing the work.  

The incident came to light after nearby residents noticed the activity and intervened. Photographs and videos of the patients cleaning the pit subsequently circulated widely. The pit was later cleaned using municipal machinery.  

The hospital’s administrative medical officer, Dr. Shankar Y. Hiregowdar, and senior nursing officer Vanitha Kurundawad were suspended by Karnataka’s Health and Family Welfare Services Department pending a departmental inquiry. According to the government order reported by India Today and PTI, the nurse was alleged to have instructed patients known to her and their relatives to manually clean the hospital cesspit, while Dr. Hiregowdar was held responsible for allowing the incident to take place.  

A police case was also registered at Savanur Police Station. Reports state that the case invokes Section 125 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita along with provisions of the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013, which prohibits the employment of people for manual removal of human excreta.  

There was also a prior warning about the sanitation problem. According to police, the cesspit had begun overflowing and Dr. Hiregowdar had written to municipal authorities on August 27, a day before the reported incident, requesting assistance. Police said no response had been received before the patients were allegedly made to undertake the cleaning.  

The departmental inquiry is intended to establish the circumstances and responsibility for what happened. The allegations should therefore be distinguished from findings that may emerge from the investigation.

No patient should have to perform hazardous sanitation work in order to receive medical care. Human dignity cannot be conditional on access to treatment.

Sources: The Indian Express, India Today, Hindustan Times, PTI/Deccan Chronicle, Salar News.

I asked Grok to help me summarize and visualize the current path NHTSA is on regarding Autonomous Vehicle (AV) Regulatory Initiatives that are and will be vital for @Tesla Cybercab and @Robotaxi along with other similar approaches like @Waymo and here is the short discussion with a table showing likely timeframes. 

NHTSA AV rules: what’s already moving vs. what’s still talk
The incremental FMVSS updates that drop human-control assumptions are already in official process, not rhetoric. 

NPRMs went out March–June 2026 on FMVSS 102, 103/104, 110, and 135 (separate tracks for no-steer/no-pedal vehicles, same core metrics like stopping distance). Comments closed late August. Agency is drafting finals with “deliberative urgency.” 

These are deregulatory (delete design specs, don’t add new ones), so 0–180 day effective dates are plausible. Simpler ones could land early 2027; the brake rule (135) more likely mid-2027. High odds they become policy: they match the admin’s AV Framework, keep safety performance, and rest on years of NHTSA ADS research.

New voluntary guidance to replace 2017 AV 2.0 is slower and lower-risk. Docket opened July 2026; chapters (emergency responders, SMS, remote assistance) planned incrementally, comments through July 2027, then a consolidated doc. Non-binding, so high chance it issues and low chance of successful suit.

The big ADS performance FMVSS announced March 2026 is the least certain. No NPRM yet. NHTSA signed the 3-year, $5M ASCEND consortium with SAE on Sept 16, 2026 to build data-driven behavioral metrics. 

Earlier talk pointed at 2028 for a full framework. Objective, repeatable, practicable tests that meet the Safety Act are hard; no country has a full FMVSS-style ADS competency standard yet. Modest chance of a robust, enforceable rule in two years. More likely: consortium metrics, an ANPRM, or continued use of defect/recall authority.

Federal preemption of “state chaos” is limited by current law. Existing FMVSS already preempt conflicting state standards on the same aspect of performance/equipment. A future ADS performance FMVSS would constrain different design/competency rules for those functions. 

Broader preemption of operational rules (where/when AVs can run, licensing, traffic enforcement) needs new legislation like SELF DRIVE Act versions, those have repeatedly stalled and have very low enactment odds. States keep substantial ops authority. That’s why the ADS standard was framed as reducing, not instantly ending, the patchwork.

Lawsuits have a moderate-to-high chance of delaying the incremental FMVSS changes (APA claims: failed to show they “meet the need for motor vehicle safety,” insufficient real-world data, arbitrary). Courts often grant 12–24 month stays. 

Lower chance they permanently kill them. Safety groups, some AGs, and labor have already criticized pace and lack of mandatory ADS behavioral standards. 

Tesla Cybercab Special Order (response due Sept 30, 2026) is a live enforcement action under current text; if NHTSA finalizes the 135 amendment first, some of those issues become moot. Broader statutory preemption would face multi-year fights from states over police-power traffic/ops authority. Defect investigations and recalls stay available either way.

This is the clearest public signal yet that NHTSA is moving the steering-wheel/pedal FMVSS track and trying to preempt state chaos with a federal ADS performance rule. Cybercab Special Order (Sep 30) still sits on a different, harder edge of that same fight.

This is what’s happening in the video. 

NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison’s Thesis: “Deliberative urgency.” Safety first, but don’t let legacy rules freeze driverless tech.

What he’s actually doing:

1. New voluntary AV guidance to replace Trump-era AV 2.0 (2017), aimed at mid-scale driverless deployments (emergency responders, SMS, remote assist).

2. Amendments to five FMVSS so vehicles without traditional steering wheels/pedals can certify; shifting from design specs to performance requirements (finals being drafted).

3. New ADS performance FMVSS (kicked off in March) with objective behavioral metrics.

4. Ascend Consortium with SAE, signed “yesterday,” to build data-driven ADS standards fast.

5. Federal lead vs state patchwork, he wants one national performance framework, not 50 different AV rules.

Enforcement stays live: investigations, recalls, and a call-out on AVs interfering with first responders. Framed under Sec. Duffy’s “Golden Era of Transportation.”

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

Foreign VPNs have often been found involved in planning & execution of terror activities, funding, facilitation and radicalisation of youth and crime against children & women by spread of p€rverted content & therefore the biggest threat to the nation's security and culture. Below is my letter to GOI seeking an immediate ban on foreign VPNs & detailing instances of their blatant misuse for:

A. Terrorism and radicalisation
B. Crime against children and women
C. Financial fraud
D. Drug trafficking
E. Extortion, blackmailing, etc.

In my letter I have listed a sample of 50 serious instances of these crimes and terror activities from India and around the world.

Below is the full text of the letter :

10th November 2025

Shri Amit Shah
Union Home Minister

Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw
Union Minister of Electronics and Information Technology

Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal
Union Minister of State (I/C) for Law & Justice

Smt Annpurna Devi
Union Minister of Women and Child Development

Sub: Urgent Request for Immediate Nationwide Ban on Foreign VPN Services to Curb Crimes Against Children, Women, Drug Trafficking, Financial Fraud, and Threats to National Security

Dear Shri Amit Shah Ji,

Namaste.

I write as a concerned citizen to bring to your urgent attention the direct role of foreign VPN services in enabling heinous crimes against children, women, and acts of terrorism—crimes that are actively bypassing existing Indian laws. Section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, via directions issued on 28 April 2022, imposes a mandatory 5-year logging requirement on VPN providers.

Despite the mandatory 5-year logging requirement imposed on VPN providers under these directions, major foreign VPNs—NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, ProtonVPN, Mullvad, and others—have openly refused compliance by removing physical servers from India and routing traffic through virtual IPs abroad. This deliberate non-cooperation has turned these services into safe havens for criminals and terrorists operating in and targeting India.

For example, the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog, Financial Action Task Force (FATF), reported on July 8, 2025, that the accused in two recent terror attacks in India—the Gorakhnath Temple attack in Uttar Pradesh on April 3, 2022, and the Pulwama suicide-bomb attack in February 2019, which killed 40 CRPF personnel—used online payment services, e-commerce platforms, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

The list of crimes and terror-related incidents involving VPNs is long. We are listing below just a few recent examples of how VPNs were used to commit crimes against children and women, plan terrorist activities, traffic drugs and conduct fraud. Each incident lists the crime, VPN use, and primary-source link [U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) / Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) / European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) / The International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol)].

Crimes Against Children (VPN-Enabled Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) Cases)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs (or VPN + Tor) to hide while committing Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) related crimes—downloading, sharing, or live-streaming.

1. Connecticut, USA – 2025
Michael Hull (61) used paid VPN + Tor for 4 years to access dark-web CSAM. FBI traced via VPN IP leak → DOJ
2. Minnesota, USA – Operation Grayskull, 2025
Thomas Katsampes (52) ran a 2,000-user CSAM forum requiring VPN + Tor hopping. FBI de-anonymized 18 admins via logs → DOJ
3. Florida, USA – Playpen Network, 2023–2025
956 arrests; 214 used NordVPN/PIA/Mullvad + Tor. FBI NIT malware captured real IPs on CSAM clicks → FBI
4. Germany – Boystown Takedown, 2021 (ongoing 2023 arrests)
400,000 users; rules mandated VPN + Tor. BKA arrested 72; 2 VPN providers surrendered logs under EU warrants → BKA/Europol
5. South Korea – Welcome to Video, 2019–2024
337 arrests; 41 used VPN exits in Sweden/Romania for Bitcoin CSAM buys. IRS traced VPN payments → DOJ
6. Australia – Childs Play, 2016–2017 (2023 follow-ups)
1.1M users; admin taught 3-VPN chaining + Tor. Task Force Argos caught 94 via VPN leaks → Queensland Police
7. Latin America – Operation Vibora, 2025
20 arrests; suspects used free mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder) for live-streamed child rape. VPN logs seized → Interpol
8. Oklahoma, USA – Thomas Gailus, 2025
Repeat offender used dark web via VPN to collect CSAM of prepubescents. 10-year sentence → DOJ
9. Washington, USA – Operation Restore Justice, 2025
Mitchell Dufault distributed CSAM via VPN-masked platforms. 10-year sentence → DOJ
10. Arizona, USA – 22 Defendants, 2023–2025
Multiple offenders used VPNs for CSAM possession/distribution. Charges under Project Safe Childhood → DOJ

Crimes Against Women (VPN-Enabled Cyberstalking/Sextortion)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs for cyberstalking, sextortion, or non-consensual porn against women.

1. Massachusetts, USA – James Florence Jr, 2025
Cyberstalked 13 women with paid VPNs for deepfake nudes/rape threats. 9-year sentence → DOJ
2. Albuquerque, USA – Phillip Gonzales, 2025
Sent rape-fantasy texts to 7 women via VPN-chained VoIP. VPN logs seized → DOJ
3. Global – 911 S5 Botnet, 2025
YunHe Wang sold VPN-proxied IPs for 4,000+ sextortion/rape threats against women. Servers seized → DOJ
4. Los Angeles, USA – Kody Roberts, 2023
Sent rape/murder threats to 3 women via commercial VPN. NIT grabbed IP → DOJ
5. Florida, USA – Christopher Buonocore, 2021–2024
Sextorted dozens, hired rapists via NordVPN + Tor. Bitcoin traces led to arrest → DOJ
6. Washington DC, USA – Nahvarj Mills, 2024
Posted revenge porn via Swedish VPN exits. 27-count indictment → DOJ
7. Naperville, USA – Cody Ratliff, 2025
Sextorted teen girl via mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder). Logs handed over → Police
8. California, USA – Chavarri Sextortion, 2019–2021 (2025 arrest)
Stalked/harassed women via VPN-masked accounts for nudes → DOJ
9. Global – Financial Sextortion Surge, 2023–2025
Overseas offenders used VPNs for anonymous threats; 33.5M losses → FinCEN/FBI
10. Nigeria – Operation Artemis, 2025
22 arrests for sextortion using VPNs to mask ops; 54K teen victims → FBI

Terrorism (VPN-Enabled Plots/Propaganda)

Here are 10 cases where terrorists used VPNs for propaganda, recruitment, or planning.

1. ISIS Global Propaganda – 2024
9 admins ran 150+ servers with https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM mandatory. FBI/Europol seized; logs exposed → FBI/Europol
2. Terrorgram Collective – 2024
Leaders used Mullvad + Tor for kill lists/bomb manuals. Payment slip traced → DOJ
3. Al-Qaeda Inspire Distributors – 2023–2025
14-cell used https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM for bomb tutorials. 3-year logs seized → Europol
4. Hamas Crypto-Fundraising – 2025
3 operatives laundered $2M via DoubleVPN Sweden exits. Logs identified wallets → DOJ
5. ISIS Sniper Channel – Minnesota, 2025
Abdelhamid Hassan uploaded 200+ videos via Safe-Inet VPN. Logs showed 18 US IPs → DOJ
6. The Base Bomb Cell – Germany/USA, 2024
5 neo-Nazis plotted via Insorg VPN C2. Logs named all → DOJ/Europol
7. Hamas Live-Stream Recruiters – Spain, 2025
9 operatives streamed via VPN-chained apps. Turbo VPN logs revealed 73 → Eurojust
8. EU Jihadist Plots – 2023–2024
24 plots (6 attacks) used VPNs for online radicalization post-Hamas Oct 7 → Europol TE-SAT
9. Al-Qaeda Online Jihad – 2023
Propaganda surge via VPN-masked uploads after Zawahiri death → Europol
10. Hamas/Al-Qassam Finance – 2025
3 campaigns dismantled; VPNs obscured cyber-finance for arms → DOJ

Other Serious Threats (VPN-Enabled Ransomware/Fraud/Etc.)

Here are 10 cases of VPN use in ransomware, hacks, fraud, murder-for-hire, drug trafficking (no overlap with prior categories).

1. ALPHV/BlackCat – US Firms, 2023
3 hackers used Mullvad/ProtonVPN for $5M ransomware. Wallet traced → DOJ
2. LockBit Hospital Attacks – TX/CA, 2024
Teen chained Nord/ExpressVPN to encrypt MRIs; 400GB leaked. Servers seized → Europol
3. $20M Real-Estate Fraud – 400 Homes, 2021–2024
Nigerian gang used IPVanish/Surfshark to divert wires. $3.2M seized → DOJ
4. Iranian Murder-for-Hire – NYC, 2024
IRGC hitmen used https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM for $100K Bitcoin scouting. Logs seized → DOJ
5. DoubleVPN – 100+ Gangs, 2019–2021
Conti/REvil used DoubleVPN for C2; 2.5K exposed via 2TB logs → Europol
6. Safe-Inet – Hive/Dharma, 2020–2025
71-country hits; Safe-Inet mandatory. BKA warrant on logs → Europol
7. Dark-Web Fentanyl Cartel – 50K Deaths, 2023–2025
Pharma-Master used VPNLab/Mullvad for 12 markets; 34 arrests → DOJ
8. DoppelPaymer Ransomware – 37 Attacks, 2023
Ukrainian core used VPNs for €10M hospital hacks (Düsseldorf). 5 arrested → Europol
9. Operation RapTor – Dark Web Drugs, 2025
288 vendors arrested; VPNs masked trafficking. €184M seized → Europol
10. MATRIX Encrypted Platform – 2024
Drug/arms/murder-for-hire via VPN-integrated comms. 2.3M messages intercepted → Europol

Foreign VPN Use in Crimes in India (2020–2025)

Here are 10 news reports from 2020–2025 detailing cases where foreign VPNs (or non-compliant international VPN services) were used to commit or facilitate crimes against children (CSAM/pornography), women (sextortion/cyberstalking), terrorism/national security threats, or other serious offenses (ransomware/fraud/drug trafficking) in India. Each includes a brief summary, crime type, and primary source link.

1. Sharp Rise in CSAM Demand via VPNs (2020)
During COVID-19 lockdown, ICPF report noted a 100% surge in child pornography searches (5M/month across 100 cities), with users employing foreign VPNs to bypass India's CSAM bans.
Crime: Child exploitation → Times of India
2. 25,000 CSAM Uploads Traced, VPNs Suspected in Access (2020)
NCMEC alerted NCRB to 25,000 child pornography uploads from India (Delhi tops list); offenders used foreign VPNs to access dark web sites, leading to FIRs and arrests in multiple states.
Crime: Child pornography distribution → The Indian Express
3. Kerala P-Hunt Operation: 47 Arrests for Dark Web CSAM (2020)
Kerala Police's covert op arrested 47 (including youth) for downloading child abuse material via foreign VPNs on darknet during lockdown; surge linked to encrypted access tools.
Crime: Child sexual abuse material → India Today
4. Porn Blackmail via VPN-Tracked Footprints (2020)
Mumbai racketeers used foreign VPNs to track porn viewers' digital footprints, then extorted bitcoins threatening exposure; cyber cell devising VPN blocks for such crimes.
Crime: Sextortion/extortion against adults (linked to child porn access) → Mumbai Mirror
5. Nagpur: 30 Arrests in 38 CSAM Cases via VPN Access (2021)
City police arrested 30 in 38 child pornography cases based on cyber intel; offenders used international VPNs to browse dark net/paid sites, prompted by NCCRP tips.
Crime: Child pornography possession → Times of India
6. Telangana: 43 Arrested for CSAM Circulation via VPNs (2023)
Cyber Crime wing arrested 43 using tip lines; suspects employed foreign VPNs to upload/share child sexual abuse material on social media/dark web.
Crime: Child pornography trafficking → The Hindu
7. Gorakhnath Temple Attack: ISIL Funding via PayPal & VPNs (2022, reported 2025)
Accused used foreign VPNs to obscure IP while transferring ₹6.7L via PayPal to ISIL supporters abroad for terror planning; FATF highlighted as national security threat.
Crime: Terrorism financing → The Hindu
8. Flight Bomb Hoax Threats via VPN-Masked IPs (2024)
Over 150 Delhi flights received hoax bomb threats on X; sender used foreign VPNs (IPs traced to London/Germany) to hide origin, complicating national security probes.
Crime: Terrorism hoax/threat to aviation security → India Today
9. Scamsters Use Rented Foreign VPNs for Ransomware/Phishing (2023)
Gujarat fraudsters rented VPNs from Marshall Islands/Australia to mask ops in ransomware, card fraud, and sextortion targeting Indians; evaded extradition via non-treaty nations.
Crime: Ransomware/financial fraud → Times of India
10. Bengaluru Rs 49Cr Fraud: Foreign Hackers Use VPN for Mule Accounts (2025)
Hackers from abroad used VPNs to breach Whizdm Finance's API, siphoning ₹49Cr via 100s of transactions; locals arrested for creating VPN-masked mule accounts.
Crime: Cyber fraud/ransomware-like theft → Times of India

Sir, the pattern is undeniable:

- Foreign VPNs openly defy Indian law.
- They enable child exploitation, pornography, violence against women, radicalization, drug trafficking and terrorist activity.

Requested Immediate Possible Actions for Consideration:

1. Publish a National Registry of Compliant VPNs
Direct CERT-In and MeitY to publish and maintain a public registry of VPN providers that have demonstrated compliance with the 28 April 2022 CERT-In Directions issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Requirement: Five-year data logging, real-time incident reporting, and appointment of an Indian-resident nodal officer.
Purpose: Establish transparency and a verifiable compliance benchmark for enforcement.

2. Delist and Prohibit Operation of Non-Compliant Foreign VPNs
Instruct Apple, Google, and all Indian ISPs to immediately delist and block all non-compliant foreign VPNs, including NordVPN, ProtonVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, and Mullvad, that have refused to adhere to the 2022 CERT-In Directions.
Action: To be taken under the blocking powers of the Information Technology Act and its associated Intermediary Guidelines.
Purpose: Prevent evasion of Indian jurisdiction and close routes for offenders hiding behind virtual foreign IPs.

3. Block Associated Payment Channels
Direct the Reserve Bank of India and all licensed payment aggregators and card networks such as PayU, Razorpay, Visa, and Mastercard to suspend or block subscription transactions to banned or non-compliant VPN providers.
Purpose: Cut off domestic funding and revenue flows sustaining illegal VPN operations.

4. Mandate Exclusive Use of CERT-In Certified VPNs
Require, through regulatory notification, that only VPNs, whether Indian or foreign, that obtain CERT-In certification be permitted to operate in India.
All VPNs advertising Indian IP services must maintain logging infrastructure within Indian jurisdiction and comply with lawful requests from enforcement agencies.
Purpose: Ensure traceability and lawful accountability of all VPN activity associated with Indian IP addresses.

5. Criminalise Intentional Use for Concealment During Offences
Propose suitable amendments or notifications under the Information Technology Act and India’s relevant penal codes to criminalise the intentional use of banned or non-compliant VPNs for concealing identity during the commission of cognisable offences involving child sexual abuse material, terrorism, radicalisation, or financial fraud.
Purpose: Target deliberate misuse while preserving lawful privacy.

6. Strengthen Traceability and Cooperation
Mandate that every VPN provider operating in India:
(a) Designate a resident nodal officer;
(b) Retain subscriber and metadata for five years; and
(c) Respond to law enforcement requests within seventy-two hours, as required by the CERT-In Directions of 2022.
Purpose: Guarantee swift investigatory access while preserving due process.

7. Establish a National Honeypot and Canarytoken Programme
Authorise CERT-In and the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit to deploy a nationwide honeypot and Canarytoken framework, as validated in peer-reviewed research, to trace VPN-enabled crimes involving child sexual abuse material, sextortion, ransomware, and terror financing.
Ensure judicial oversight, privacy protection, and certified chain of custody for admissibility of digital evidence.
Purpose: Build indigenous technical capability to unmask offenders using VPN anonymity.

8. Strengthen International Coordination and FATF Alignment
Direct NIA, CBI, and MHA’s Cyber Coordination Centre to:
(a) Formalise fast-track cooperation with FBI, Europol, and Interpol under Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties; and
(b) Report VPN-linked money-laundering or terror-financing incidents to the Financial Action Task Force in conformity with its Comprehensive Update on Terrorist Financing Risks dated 8 July 2025.
Purpose: Integrate India’s enforcement with global counter-terror and cybercrime frameworks.

9. Institute Annual CERT-In Audit and Enforcement Schedule
Require annual audits of VPN providers’ compliance and publish audit summaries for public accountability.
Providers failing to comply beyond sixty days after notice should face permanent blocking and notifications to RBI, DoT, and MeitY for coordinated enforcement.
Purpose: Ensure continuous oversight and eliminate recurring non-compliance.

10. Issue a Public Advisory and Compliance Deadline
Issue a national advisory within thirty days, notifying all VPN providers of a sixty-day compliance window.
After the deadline, non-compliant entities should face delisting, domain blocking, and payment interdiction without exception.
Purpose: Provide procedural fairness before enforcement action begins.

India must not remain a playground for foreign tools that shield sexual predators, criminals and terrorists. The Ministry of Home Affairs has already acted strictly—forcing Apple and Google to delist 6+ non-compliant VPNs in January 2025. It is time to complete the job.

Vande Mataram

Uday Mahurkar
Founder, Save Culture Save Bharat Foundation
Former Central Information Commissioner, Government of India

Shri PK Mishra, Principal Secretary to PM
Shri Govind Mohan, Home Secretary
Shri S. Krishnan, Secretary (E&IT)
Dr. Anju Rathi Rana, Law Secretary
Shri Anil Malik, Secretary, Ministry of Women & Child Development

text:
IFF Statement: Blocking of the Cockroach Janta Party's Instagram account

July 22, 2026

The Instagram account of the Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) is no longer accessible to users in India. Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

We emphasise that the account is primarily engaged in acts of political speech that enjoy the full protection of Article 19(1)(a). The account has been restricted after the movement's march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak, and while the Delhi High Court examines allegations of excessive police force against protesters. Viewed in this background the blocking of its social media account at this moment is the suppression of dissent.

The secrecy compounds the illegality. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act on the strength of its procedural safeguards. In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We also note that Meta's notice refers to a "legal request", not an order.  We call on MeitY to disclose the order, furnish a copy to the account holder, and provide a hearing. We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

text:
Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.
